info.description:
The AerScheduler REST API. Schedule aircraft, close flights out, invoice them, and pull the numbers back — from your own software.

## Getting started

**The API is used with an API key**, and only with an API key.

Create one in the web console at **Settings → API keys**. Give it a name you'll
recognise and tick the roles it needs. The secret is shown once, at that moment,
and is never retrievable again — we store only a hash.

The roles a key may hold are `admin`, `dispatcher`, `instructor`, `student`,
`renter` and `technician`. `owner` cannot be granted to a key. Give a key the
least it needs — one that reads the schedule is a `dispatcher`, not an
`admin` — because every permission rule that applies to a person holding those
roles applies to the key.

Revoking is in the same place, and takes effect on the very next request.

**Key management is deliberately absent from the reference below**, and that is
not an oversight. `/apiKeys` is the one part of this API a key cannot use: a key
cannot create, list or revoke a key, even one holding the admin role. If it
could, a single leaked key would be a permanent foothold — you revoke it and
whatever took it has already issued itself three more. So those routes answer
403 to a key, and documenting them beside endpoints that work would be a trap.
Everything in the reference works with the credential this page tells you to use.

Everything after that — every request your software makes — uses the key:

```bash
export AERSCHEDULER_KEY=ask_live_…

curl -s https://api.aerscheduler.com/resources/planes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AERSCHEDULER_KEY"
```

That is the whole setup. There is no sign-in step and no token to refresh: a key
is a long-lived credential you store once, and it keeps working until you revoke
it or its expiry passes.

Keys carry **roles**, so a key is scoped to what it actually needs. A key that
reads the schedule should be a `dispatcher`, not an `admin`. Every permission
rule that applies to a person holding those roles applies to the key.

Creating and revoking keys requires a signed-in administrator — a key cannot mint
another key, so a leaked key cannot issue itself replacements.

## Conventions

Every one of these holds across the whole API, so you can write one client wrapper and stop thinking about it:

- **Responses are wrapped.** A body-bearing success is `{ "data": … }`. An error is `{ "message": "…" }`, and the message is written to be safe to show a user. A few endpoints noted individually break this: `/health`, the CSV export, and the OAuth redirects.
- **Status codes mean what they say.** `200` read or update, `201` created, `204` done with nothing to return, `400` your request was wrong, `401` sign in again, `403` signed in but not allowed, `404` no such thing, `429` slow down.
- **`401` and `403` are different.** `401` means the token is dead — get a new one. `403` means the token is fine and the answer is still no; retrying will not help.
- **Collections are `GET /thing`, items are `GET /thing/{id}`.** Create is `POST` to the collection, update is `PATCH` to the item, delete is `DELETE` on the item. Where a resource deviates, the endpoint says so.
- **Your organization is implied.** The token carries it. You never pass an organization id, and you can never read another organization's records.
- **Ids are integers** and stable for the life of the record.
- **Money is in cents**, as an integer. Never a float.

## Time zones

Scheduling is anchored to the **airport's** time zone, not the caller's device. A booking made at 7am at the field is 7am at the field regardless of where the person making it happens to be.

In practice that means: send `start` and `end` with an **explicit UTC offset or `Z`**. A bare local datetime like `2026-08-04T15:00:00` is rejected — it would be read in the server's zone and silently book a different instant than the person picked. Send `timeZoneName` (an IANA zone) alongside so the booking knows which zone it was made in.

## Reservation types

Which `type` a caller may create depends on the roles they hold. Roles are additive: an instructor who is also a technician may create both sets.

| Role | May create |
|---|---|
| owner, admin, dispatcher | solo, dual, ground, guest, sim, rental, maintenance |
| instructor | solo, dual, ground, guest, sim |
| student | solo, dual, ground, sim |
| renter | rental |
| technician | maintenance |

## Rate limits

Limits are applied per signed-in account, not per IP, so a whole school behind one office address does not share one budget.

| | Limit |
|---|---|
| Per account | 300 requests/minute, 5,000/hour |
| Unauthenticated | 100 requests per 5 minutes, per IP |
| Unauthenticated endpoints | Tighter still, and limited per IP |

Every response carries `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset`. A `429` carries `Retry-After` in seconds — honour it rather than retrying on a fixed interval.

## Pagination

**Every list is capped at 1,000 rows**, whether or not you ask for a limit. Pass `limit` and `offset` to page:

```
GET /reservations?startDate=…&endDate=…&limit=100&offset=200
```

Every list response carries a `pagination` object beside `data`:

```json
{
  "data": [ … ],
  "pagination": { "total": 7823, "limit": 1000, "offset": 0, "returned": 1000, "hasMore": true }
}
```

- `total` — how many there are in all, before the page was taken.
- `returned` — how many are in `data` right now.
- `hasMore` — whether another page exists. **Check it.** It is how you find out a collection is bigger than one page, and some of ours are: our largest school has over 7,000 reservations.

Asking for more than 1,000 gives you 1,000 rather than an error, so you never need to know the ceiling to write a working request. `offset` past the end returns an empty `data` and `hasMore: false`.

Cursor pagination is coming and will be additive — `limit`/`offset` will keep working.

### Ordering

`sort` names a field to order by, as a dot path into the row, and `order` is `asc` (the default) or `desc`:

```
GET /invoices?sort=total&order=desc&limit=50
```

**Sort here rather than after you receive the page.** Ordering is applied to the whole collection before the page is cut, so `sort=total&order=desc&limit=50` gives you the fifty largest invoices. Sorting the page yourself orders the fifty rows you happen to be holding, which is a different — and usually wrong — answer.

Numbers order as numbers and ISO timestamps as instants, so `total` does not put `1000` before `90`. Empty values sort last in both directions: an invoice with no `paidAt` is not the most recent payment. Ties keep the endpoint's own order, so paging a sort by a coarse field like status will not skip or repeat rows.

Omit `sort` and you get the order the endpoint has always used.

## Versioning

**The unprefixed paths are v1.** `https://api.aerscheduler.com/reservations` is the v1 reservations endpoint; there is no `/v1/` to add and adding one will 404. That is deliberate — a version segment you never change is decoration, and we would rather not pretend.

This document describes **v1.0.0**, which you can read at `info.version` in the spec.

**What can change under you, without notice:**

- New endpoints.
- New fields on an existing response.
- New optional request parameters.
- New values in an enum you are already handling.

So parse leniently: ignore fields you do not recognise, and do not assume an enum is closed. An integration that breaks when we add a field is an integration that will break.

**What will never change within v1:**

- An endpoint disappearing, or moving.
- A field disappearing from a response, or changing type.
- A previously optional request parameter becoming required.
- A success status code changing.

Anything in that second list means **v2**, which would be served alongside v1 at `/v2/…` rather than replacing it. You would get notice by email before it existed, and v1 would keep working for a stated period afterwards — we are not going to break a customer's software to save ourselves a route table.

**Deprecations** are announced in the changelog and carry a `Deprecation` header on the affected endpoint before anything is removed.

patch.description:
Retires somebody from the roster, or brings them back. Requires the **admin** role — a dispatcher cannot.

An archived member **is not notified, ever** — no email, no push, no in-app notice. They are left out of `GET /orgUsers` unless you pass `archived=true` (which is also how you list them again), and they cannot be added to a booking. Nothing is deleted: their flights, invoices and history are untouched, and restoring them is the same call with `false`.

Use this rather than grounding to tidy a roster. **Grounding is a live restriction and emails the member**, so grounding a batch of people who stopped flying years ago sends each of them an unexpected notice.

Books a resource, a person, or both.

`start` and `end` **must carry an explicit UTC offset or `Z`**. A bare local datetime is rejected: it would be read in the server's zone and silently book a different instant than the customer picked.

Which `type` values you may create depends on your roles — see the Reservation types section. The server also refuses double-bookings and bookings on grounded aircraft.

Pass a `recurrence` object to create a repeating series. Occurrences are real reservations, so each one can be ramped, reviewed, and invoiced independently.

personnel.description:
Who is on the booking. One person cannot fill two seats on the same booking.

**Several people may share a side.** How many depends on the booking type: a `ground` class takes up to 12 students, `sim` up to 6, `dual` and `solo` up to 4, and `rental` up to 4 renters. `maintenance` takes nobody and `guest` takes one guest. Exceeding a limit is a 400 naming the side and the number allowed.

**Order matters.** The first person on a side is the leading payer: they are billed when the organization's rule for a charge is "one person pays", and they take the remainder cent of an uneven division.

Everyone listed must be free for the slot and must meet the currency and grounding rules — the booking is refused naming whoever does not, not silently trimmed.

post.description:
Generates the bill for a closed-out flight. Requires the **admin** role.

**Returns an ARRAY.** A booking shared between several people produces one invoice PER PAYER — a Stripe invoice bills exactly one customer, so splitting a booking's cost has to be several invoices rather than one invoice with shares underneath it. A booking with one payer returns an array of one.

How the cost divides is set per organization and per booking type — see the cost-splitting rules in the console. With no rules configured, one person is billed for the whole booking, which is how this endpoint has always behaved.

**Partial success is possible and is not an error.** If the payment processor accepts some invoices and rejects another, the ones that succeeded are real and are returned, with a `warnings` array naming who could not be billed. Call this endpoint again to bill only the payers who still have no invoice — it will not duplicate the ones already raised. A 400 means nothing was billed at all.

A share below the processor's 50-cent minimum is skipped rather than raised, and reported in `warnings`.

400.description: The flight is not closed out, every payer is already invoiced, or the organization's split rules cannot be applied to it — for example a booking set to split by each person's own time where somebody's hours have not been entered. The message says what to fix.

put.description:
Records each person's stake in the cost of a booking: their own meter readings when the charge is split by the time each person flew, their percentage when it is split by set shares, or a waiver for somebody who is on the booking but owes nothing (a safety pilot).

**Replaces the whole set.** Shares have to total 100% across everybody, so merging one person into an existing set is how a total quietly stops adding up. Send everybody every time.

Only people already on the booking may be given a stake. Refused once the booking has been invoiced — the invoices describe the hours and shares they were computed from, and rewriting those underneath them would leave the money disagreeing with its own record.

Whether the shares total 100%, and whether the individual meter readings add up to what the aircraft actually ran, is checked when the booking is INVOICED rather than here — so a half-finished close-out can still be saved.

bearerAuth.description:
An API key, sent as `Authorization: Bearer ask_live_…`.

Create one in the web console at **Settings → API keys**. The secret is shown once and stored only as a hash — if you lose it, revoke the key and create another.

A key is scoped to one organization and carries the roles you gave it — every permission rule that applies to a member holding those roles applies to the key. Grant the least it needs.

coordinates.description: Geocoded position, when the address could be resolved.

ApiKey.description: A credential that lets software act on your organization's behalf. The secret is never included — only a hash is stored.

id.description: Unique identifier, stable for the life of the record.

prefix.description: The displayable head of the key. Not a secret, and not enough to reconstruct one.

roles.description: What the key can do. These are real roles — every rule that applies to a member holding them applies to the key.

expiresAt.description: When it stops working. Null means no expiry.

revokedAt.description: When it was revoked. Null while live.

lastUsedAt.description: When it last authenticated a request, to the nearest minute. Null if never used — which is how you find keys to turn off.

createdBy.description: The administrator who minted it. Null if they have since left.

ApiKeyWithSecret.description: A newly created key. This is the ONLY response that ever contains the secret — store it now.

id.description: Unique identifier, stable for the life of the record.

prefix.description: The displayable head of the key.

secret.description: The key itself. Send it as `Authorization: Bearer <secret>`. We store only a hash, so if you lose this you must revoke the key and mint another.

Pagination.description: Where this page sits in the whole collection. Present on every list response.

total.description: How many there are in all, before this page was taken.

limit.description: Rows requested for this page. 1000 unless you asked for fewer.

offset.description: Rows skipped to reach this page.

hasMore.description: Whether another page exists. Check this — some collections are larger than one page.

id.description: Unique identifier, stable for the life of the record.

showInDirectory.description: Whether this location appears in the public directory.

timeZone.description: IANA time zone of the field, e.g. `America/Denver`. Scheduling is anchored to the AIRPORT's zone, not the caller's device — see the Time zones section.

coordinates.description: Geocoded position, when the address could be resolved.

Plane.description: Aircraft-specific detail on a resource whose type is a plane.

categoryClass.description: One of `single-engine land`, `multi-engine land`, `single-engine sea`, `multi-engine sea`.

rampedIn.description: True when the aircraft is on the ramp and available.

grounded.description: True when the aircraft is unavailable for booking.

fuelEngine2.description: Fuel on board, engine 2, for twins.

dryRate.description: Dry rate per hour, in cents.

wetRate.description: Wet rate per hour, in cents.

overnightMinimumTenths.description:
This aircraft's least billable time per night away, in TENTHS of an hour, applied as a floor on a booking that spans nights. `20` bills at least 2.0 hours a night.

`null` means inherit the organization's figure; `0` means exempt this aircraft entirely. The two are not interchangeable — an exempt aircraft must stay exempt when the school-wide figure changes.

Resource.description: Anything that can be booked: an aircraft, a simulator, or a room. The `type` object carries whichever detail applies.

id.description: Unique identifier, stable for the life of the record.

type.description: Exactly one of these is populated.

User.description: A person. One account can belong to many organizations.

id.description: Unique identifier, stable for the life of the record.

email.description: Email address. Unique across the system.

emailVerifiedAt.description: When the address was verified. Null means unverified.

UserDetails.description: A person's contact record. Returned only to the person themselves, an admin or dispatcher of your organization, or an instructor the person is assigned to as a student — so expect it to be absent on most reads.

phone.description: Primary, SMS-capable number, in **E.164** (`+13035551234`). Numbers sent to this API are normalized to E.164 on write and rejected if they are not real, dialable numbers; a number with no country code is read as US unless you send `defaultCountry`.

phoneCountry.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country of `phone`, so it can be re-rendered nationally.

dateOfBirth.description: Date of birth, `YYYY-MM-DD`. A calendar date — no time, no zone.

preferredName.description: What they go by, when that isn't their legal first name.

coordinates.description: Geocoded position, when the address could be resolved.

emergencyContacts.description: Everyone on this person's emergency list, primary first.

relationship.description: How they are related. Free text.

altPhone.description: Second number to try, in E.164.

notes.description: Anything else worth knowing when calling.

isPrimary.description: True for the one to try first. At most one per person.

sortOrder.description: Display order within the person's list.

roles.description: Roles held in this organization. Additive and non-hierarchical: a person can be both instructor and technician.

archivedAt.description: When the organization retired this person from its roster; null for a current member. Archived members receive no notifications of any kind, are omitted from member lists unless asked for, and cannot be booked. Distinct from `grounded`, which is a live restriction on somebody who is still here.

id.description: Unique identifier, stable for the life of the record.

title.description: Short label shown on the calendar.

type.description: What kind of booking this is. Which types a caller may CREATE depends on their roles — see the Reservation types section.

start.description: Start instant. MUST carry an explicit offset or `Z`.

end.description:
End instant. MUST carry an explicit offset or `Z`.

MAY fall on a later calendar day than `start`. A school with multi-day bookings enabled can book a trip that keeps the resource for the whole span, and the resource is unavailable for every day in between rather than becoming free again each morning. Do not assume a booking ends on the day it starts.

timeZoneName.description: IANA zone the booking is anchored to, e.g. `America/Denver`. Resolved from the LOCATION, falling back to the organization — not from the caller's device, because how many nights a trip spans decides what it bills.

cancelledAt.description: When it was cancelled. Null for a live booking.

cancellationCategory.description: Fixed-list reason. Null on bookings cancelled before this was introduced — reports count those as “Not recorded”, not “Other”.

rrule.description: Recurrence rule, when this booking belongs to a repeating series.

invoices.description:
ONE PER PAYER. A booking shared between several people mints an invoice each — a Stripe invoice bills exactly one customer. A booking with one payer has an array of one, and an un-billed booking has an empty array.

Do not read `invoices[0]` as "the invoice": on a split booking that is one person's share. Ask whether EVERY payer has one.

invoice.description: **Deprecated — use `invoices`.** The first non-void invoice, kept so clients written before split billing keep working. On a booking with one payer this is exactly what it always meant; on a split booking it is only ONE person's share, so anything that reports whether a flight has been billed should read `invoices`. This field will be removed.

types.description: Every type this caller may search — the full category list, not just the types that matched. Narrowed by role: a member who cannot read squawks never sees `squawk` here.

results.description: The matches, grouped by type in the order of `types`.

AuditEvent.description: One recorded thing somebody did. Append-only: audit events are never edited or deleted.

action.description: Dotted and past tense — `reservation.rescheduled`, `invoice.voided`, `resource.grounded`. Stable: values are never renamed, because rows written months ago still carry the old string.

entityType.description: What kind of thing it happened to.

entityId.description: The id of that thing. Not a foreign key — an event outlives the row it describes, so this can point at something that has since been deleted.

summary.description: A finished sentence, written when the event was recorded.

changes.description: Only the fields that moved, as `{ field: { from, to } }`.

source.description: `web`, `ios`, `api`, or `system`. Null when it could not be determined.

actor.description: Who did it. Null for system-originated events.

subject.description: The member the event is about, which is usually not the actor.

resource.description: The aircraft, simulator or room it touched, if any.

Error.description: Every error response has this shape.

message.description: Human-readable explanation, safe to show a user.

retryAfter.description: Seconds to wait before retrying. Present on 429 only.
